observations.explanation: The benchmark description combines database/API interaction, a simulated user, and domain-specific policies (PDF pp. 2–4); reward compares the final database state with a ground-truth outcome and also checks user-facing outputs (p. 4).

The paper defines pass^k as the probability that all k trials succeed and presents it as a measure of consistency and robustness (PDF pp. 4–5). It reports that pass^k declines with more trials and that gpt-4o’s pass^8 is below 25% in retail (p. 7).

The paper focuses on two customer-service domains, retail and airline (PDF p. 5), and explicitly says their schemas, APIs, and rules are simplified relative to real-world domains (p. 6). It does not establish transfer to more consequential or complex settings in these experiments.

The discussion identifies limitations of the LM-simulated user and explicitly notes implicit bias from tuning the user prompt with a gpt-4-turbo function-calling agent (PDF p. 9). The paper reports no comparison against human users or independently curated tasks, so the carefully qualified question about how results would compare remains open.
